lessons.title: Health and safety duties and hazards
lessons.html:
Why monitor health and safety?

Hunting operations, lodges and farms have many hazards: firearms, dangerous animals, vehicles, knives, chemicals, heat, fire and remote locations far from hospitals. The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 (OHS Act) requires employers to provide a workplace that is safe and without risk to health as far as reasonably practicable, and requires employees to take care of their own safety and that of others.

Duties under the OHS Act (in summary)

  • Employer: identify hazards, assess risks, put controls in place, provide training, information, supervision and protective equipment, and keep machinery safe.
  • Employees: follow safety rules, use protective equipment, report unsafe conditions and incidents, and not interfere with safety equipment.
  • Health and safety representatives: in workplaces with more than 20 employees, representatives must be appointed to inspect the workplace and raise concerns.

Injuries and occupational diseases must be reported, and the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993 (COIDA) provides compensation for injured workers.

Common hazards in a hunting operation

HazardExample controls
FirearmsSafety rules, training, chamber empty in vehicles, safe storage
Dangerous animalsArmed PH present, briefings, no walking alone
Vehicles on rough roadsSpeed limits, seat belts where fitted, no riding on bonnets, maintenance
Knives in skinning shedsSharp knives, cut-resistant gloves, first aid kit
ZoonosesGloves, hygiene, report unexplained deaths
Heat and sunWater, hats, rest in shade, work early
Snakes and insectsBoots, awareness, snakebite plan

lessons.title: Monitoring, inspections and incidents
lessons.html:
Monitoring health and safety

Monitoring means checking regularly that safety controls are in place and working, and acting when they are not.

Tools for monitoring

  • Inspections with a checklist: vehicles (brakes, tyres, lights, first aid kit, fire extinguisher), skinning shed (floors, knives, hygiene), gun safe and register, kitchen and gas installations.
  • Observation: watching how people work, e.g. firearm handling in the vehicle.
  • Safety talks: short "toolbox talks" before activities.
  • Records: training, inspections, incidents, equipment servicing.
  • Feedback from staff and the health and safety representative.

Acting on findings

When you find a hazard: make it safe immediately if you can (for example, take a vehicle with faulty brakes out of service), report it to the person in charge, record it, and follow up until it is fixed.

Incidents and emergencies

  1. Make the area safe and prevent further injury.
  2. Give first aid by a trained first aider and call for medical help. Remote operations need an evacuation plan with GPS coordinates and emergency numbers.
  3. Report the incident to management. Serious incidents must be reported to the Department of Employment and Labour as the OHS Act requires.
  4. Investigate: what happened, why (root causes), and how to prevent it.
  5. Record the incident and the corrective actions.

Near misses, such as an accidental discharge that hurt nobody, must also be reported and investigated; they are warnings.

First aid readiness

Every vehicle and camp needs a stocked first aid kit, including trauma dressings for severe bleeding. Staff must be trained in first aid by an accredited provider; online learning alone is not enough.

Key points

  • The OHS Act 85 of 1993 places duties on employers and employees.
  • Major hazards include firearms, dangerous animals, vehicles, knives, zoonoses and heat.
  • Monitor through inspections, observation, safety talks and records.
  • Make hazards safe, report, record and follow up.
  • Report and investigate incidents and near misses; keep first aid ready.
